newsitem.title: UK: UK thinks the unthinkable - a Labour landslide.
newsitem.headline: UK thinks the unthinkable - a Labour landslide.

text.p: With just weeks to go before Britain's election, one word has come to hog the headlines -- landslide.
The "L" word makes Labour leader Tony Blair shudder.
The main opposition party leads the ruling Conservatives by around 20 percentage points according to recent opinion polls, enough to give it a thumping majority in parliament.
But no one in Labour has forgotten the triumphalist tone that former leader Neil Kinnock took at a rally in the northern city of Sheffield just days before the 1992 election.
With Labour's small but clear-cut poll lead holding steady, Kinnock punched the air as if victory was already assured.
When the ballots were cast, voters punched back, returning John Major's Conservatives by a comfortable margin for a fourth straight term. Kinnock quit as Labour leader soon after.
Were wavering voters put off by his apparent smugness? Did they resent being taken for granted?
Whatever the reason for the late swing from Labour, Blair is determined not to repeat Kinnock's mistakes and never misses an opportunity to warn his party not to relax.

"There is only one opinion poll that matters and that is the one on election day. I am and remain the eternal warrior against complacency. We are doing well. But we take nothing for granted," Blair told Labour's Scottish conference last Friday.
A day earlier, the Labour leader had politely but firmly refused even to discuss how his family might find living at 10 Downing Street, the prime minister's official residence.
The same message is hammered home by Blair's lieutenants.

Underlining the scale of Labour's task, Peter Mandelson, who is in charge of the party's election planning, noted that Labour would require a net uniform swing of 4.1 percent to regain power for the first time since 1979.
To secure a comfortable majority of 50, it would need a swing of six percent.

"Yet the highest swing from Conservative to Labour since 1945 was 3.2 percent in 1964. Neither major party has achieved a swing of six percent," he wrote in Tuesday's Times newspaper under the headline Don't bank on a Labour landslide'.
And yet, and yet...

Since Labour captured the hitherto safe Conservative seat of Wirral South in a by-election on February 27 with a swing of 17 percent, the political columns have been full of articles debating the pros and cons of a large Labour majority.

Even cautious Robin Cook, Labour's foreign affairs spokesman, let slip last week the hope that 1997 would witness the second Labour landslide of the century on a par with its victory in 1945 when it won a majority of well over 100 in the House of Commons, which will have 659 seats after this election.

"The general election is now Labour's to lose. It will take an avalanche to eliminate its present lead. And, if recent events are a reliable guide, we have entered territory where anything is possible, including a landslide, " Philip Stephens wrote in the Financial Times newspaper on Tuesday.

Labour strategists know their lead will narrow in the run-up to the election, widely expected on May 1, as the Conservatives' well-financed campaign moves into top gear and wavering voters return to the ruling party's fold.
But for now, Labour seems to have the government on the defensive. Its drip-feed of damaging disclosures over meat hygiene has overshadowed bold new Conservative plans to reform the welfare state.
The ruling party's news conferences this week have been desultory affairs. Labour's chief business manager or whip, Donald Dewar, admits the Wirral South victory has given the party enormous hope.
If the by-election's voting pattern was repeated at the general election, Labour would have a massive 275-seat majority in the expanded Commons, the lower chamber.
"I'll let you into a secret," he said the other day, a twinkle in his eye. "In the whips' (business managers) office, we'd settle for just over half that size."
